questions.stem: Kelly, 45, is in ED with 4 weeks of burning retrosternal pain after meals. She mentions that solid food sometimes sticks behind her breastbone. Which question best helps you tell a mechanical narrowing (stricture or cancer) from an oesophageal motility disorder?
options: "Does the pain spread to your arm, jaw or neck, or come on when you walk uphill?"
"Do you get a sour or bitter taste coming up into your mouth, especially after meals?"
"Do drinks stick as well, or only solid foods like bread or meat?"
"Is the pain worse when you lie flat or bend over, or when you wake during the night?"
questions.why: Dysphagia to solids only, especially if it is getting worse, points to a mechanical narrowing such as a peptic stricture or cancer. Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia or oesophageal spasm.
notes: Radiation to the arm, jaw or neck helps separate cardiac from oesophageal pain, but it says nothing about the cause of her dysphagia.
Acid regurgitation supports a diagnosis of GORD, but it does not tell you whether the food sticking is due to a stricture or a motility disorder.
Worse pain when lying flat or bending over points to reflux, but it does not tell you whether the dysphagia is mechanical or due to a motility disorder.

questions.stem: Kelly, 45, has had ACS ruled out in ED (normal ECG during pain, hs-troponin I 3 ng/L at 0 and 2 hours). She has typical reflux symptoms, plus 2 weeks of dysphagia to solids and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss over 3 months. What is the best plan for her GORD on discharge?
options: Urgent gastroscopy referral and start pantoprazole 40 mg daily before breakfast
Pantoprazole 40 mg daily for 8 weeks; gastroscopy only if symptoms persist after that
Urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori, then 14 days of eradication therapy if positive
Barium swallow first, then gastroscopy only if a stricture is seen on the films
questions.why: Dysphagia and unintentional weight loss are alarm features. She needs a prompt gastroscopy to look for a stricture, Barrett's oesophagus or cancer, and to take biopsies, not just a PPI trial. A standard-dose PPI before breakfast treats the reflux while she waits.
notes: An empirical PPI trial is suitable only for uncomplicated reflux. With alarm features, waiting for a response could delay the diagnosis of a stricture or cancer.
Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features. It does not investigate dysphagia or weight loss.
Gastroscopy is the first-line test for dysphagia with alarm features because it allows biopsy and treatment. A barium swallow only delays it.

questions.stem: Kelly, 45, gets burning retrosternal pain with acid regurgitation after big meals and when she lies on the couch. It is never brought on by exertion. What is the main mechanism of reflux in GORD that explains this pattern?
options: Excess gastric acid secretion overwhelming a normally competent sphincter at all times
Transient LOS relaxations triggered by gastric distension, worse without gravity
Failure of LOS relaxation with loss of peristalsis in the oesophageal body after meals
Delayed gastric emptying from vagal neuropathy raising intragastric volume after meals
questions.why: Most reflux happens during transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) that are not caused by swallowing. These are triggered by stretch receptors in the distended gastric fundus after a meal. Lying flat removes the help of gravity, so acid refluxes more easily and clears more slowly.
notes: Most people with GORD secrete a normal amount of acid. The problem is acid getting into the oesophagus, not making too much of it.
This describes achalasia, which causes dysphagia to solids and liquids and regurgitation of undigested food, not post-meal acid reflux.
Gastroparesis can make reflux worse, but it is not the main mechanism. Kelly has no early satiety, bloating or vomiting to suggest it.

questions.stem: Kelly, 45, has dysphagia and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss. As part of your examination, you palpate the left supraclavicular fossa for Virchow's node. Why do upper GI cancers typically spread to a node on the left side?
options: The right lymphatic duct drains the abdomen into the left brachiocephalic vein
Gastric lymph drains directly to the left deep cervical nodes along the left vagus
The cervical oesophagus lies left of midline, so its nodes sit in the left neck
The thoracic duct carries abdominal lymph to the left subclavian–jugular junction
questions.why: Lymph from the abdomen drains through the coeliac nodes to the cisterna chyli and then up the thoracic duct. The thoracic duct empties at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins, so tumour cells can lodge in a node in the left supraclavicular fossa.
notes: The right lymphatic duct drains only the right side of the head, neck, thorax and right upper limb. It enters the venous system on the right, not the left.
Gastric lymph drains to the left gastric and coeliac nodes and then up the thoracic duct. There is no direct path to the cervical nodes along the vagus.
Her lesion is likely in the distal oesophagus or gastro-oesophageal junction, which drains to the left gastric and coeliac nodes, not straight to the neck.
